title: Chinese tacky against European tensor rubbers
seo_title: Tacky vs tensor rubbers: Chinese and European compared
description: How Chinese tacky rubbers like Hurricane 3 differ from European and Japanese tensor rubbers, how each plays, what they cost and which suits your game.
summary: The two great families of attacking rubber grip the ball in different ways: one with a sticky surface, the other with springy, high-tension rubber. Here is what that means at the table.
key_points: Tacky rubbers have a sticky top sheet that grips the ball; DHS's Hurricane 3 is the best-known example.
Tensor (high-tension) rubbers are built with tension in the rubber and a springy sponge, so the ball leaves them quickly.
Tacky rubbers usually have hard sponge and reward a full, fast stroke; tensors give more help with less effort.
Hybrids such as Butterfly's Dignics 09C combine a tacky surface with high tension.
Any rubber must be used as the maker made it: boosting it yourself is banned.
body: Both are smooth, inverted rubbers for attacking play, but they get their grip and speed in different ways. A Chinese tacky rubber, such as DHS's Hurricane 3, has a sticky surface that holds the ball and a hard sponge, so most of the speed has to come from your own stroke. A European or Japanese tensor rubber has tension built into the rubber itself and a springy sponge, so the ball comes off faster and with less effort. Tensors are easier for most club players; tacky rubbers suit strong, well-coached strokes and a tight short game.

Inverted rubber is a top sheet of pimpled rubber, pimples facing inwards, on a layer of sponge; our guide to [rubbers explained](/guide/table-tennis-rubbers-explained.html) covers the other types. Butterfly, the Japanese maker, sorts its inverted rubbers into families. It defines a high-friction rubber as one "which imparts spin on the ball with ease as a result of the tackiness of the surface", and a high-tension rubber as one with "very high elasticity and friction", created "by impacting tension into the rubber molecule".

The two pull against each other. Butterfly says that "in general, when High Tension is applied, the adhesive performance of the sheet's surface tends to decrease". That trade-off is the main difference between the two families.
## Chinese tacky rubbers

The best-known tacky rubber is DHS's Hurricane 3, made by the Chinese company Double Happiness. A Chinese retailer describes it as "strongly tacky". Chinese retailers list it with a sponge hardness of 38 to 41 degrees, 39 or 40 being the most common, and in thicknesses of 2.15mm and 2.2mm. That is thicker and firmer than most beginners' rubbers.

DHS also sells Neo Hurricane 3, which retailers describe as the "classic tacky Hurricane 3 topsheet" on a "factory-tuned" sponge that gives more speed on full strokes. DHS's own English-language product pages could not be checked for this guide, so treat those descriptions as the sellers' rather than the maker's.
## European and Japanese tensor rubbers

"Tensor" is a trade name that has become a general term. Andro, the German brand, describes TENSOR as "a technology in which an organic substance comparable to a spring is incorporated between the rubber molecules of the rubber". Butterfly's equivalent is High Tension, which it says "enhances the reaction of the playing surface by adding tension to the rubber molecule itself", used with what it calls Spring Sponge, which "absorbs the incoming energy of the ball and releases it as additional power".

Examples include Butterfly's Tenergy 05, Tibhar's Evolution MX-P, Donic's Bluefire M1 and andro's Rasanter R47. Their surfaces grip the ball but are not sticky. Tibhar says that with the MX-P you feel a longer contact time between ball and racket, which players call dwell.
## How they play

A tensor rubber does part of the work for you. A medium-paced stroke still produces a fast, spinning ball, which makes tensors forgiving when you are not perfectly balanced or are playing away from the table.

A tacky rubber gives less back on its own. With a hard sponge, it needs a full, fast swing that brushes the ball and drives through it. When that stroke is right, the sticky surface produces heavy spin. When it is lazy, the ball comes off slowly and can drop short or into the net. The grip also helps close to the table: Butterfly says the tackiness of its Dignics 09C lets a short push stop "near the net" with a lot of spin.
## Hybrids

Several makers now sell rubbers that try to combine the two. Butterfly says its Dignics 09C was designed to have "both high reaction as a tension rubber and the high rotational performance of a tacky rubber", and credits its "ball-holding tackiness" with good control on short shots. Its European site describes the sponge as "very hard" at 44 on Butterfly's scale and says the rubber "requires considerable power from the player". Glayzer 09C is a cheaper Butterfly rubber of the same kind, with a sponge hardness of 42.
## Hardness numbers don't compare

Each maker measures hardness its own way. Butterfly says its figure "is measured by Butterfly's own standard": Tenergy 05 is 36 and Dignics 09C 44. German makers' figures read higher for rubbers of similar feel, such as 47 for the Rasanter R47 and 47.5 for the Bluefire M1, while Chinese rubbers are listed in degrees. Compare within one brand, not across them; our guide to [sponge thickness and hardness](/guide/rubber-sponge-thickness-hardness.html) explains more.
## What the rules say

Both kinds are legal if they are on the ITTF's list of authorised rubbers and used as they were made. The Laws say the covering "shall be used without any physical, chemical or other treatment". Boosters, oils that some players brushed on to the sponge to make it faster, count as treatment. The ITTF said in 2019 that such "after treatments are strictly prohibited in table tennis". Our guide to [approved rubbers and the racket rules](/guide/ittf-approved-rubbers-and-racket-rules.html) covers the detail.
## What they cost

At UK retailers, standard Hurricane 3 sells for roughly £20 to £30 a sheet, and Neo and other upgraded versions for about £25 to £55. German-made tensors such as Evolution MX-P are about £40 to £50. Tenergy is about £60, and Dignics about £80.
## Which should you choose?

If you are moving to your first [custom bat](/guide/custom-vs-ready-made-bats.html), start with a tensor or a softer, all-round rubber in medium thickness. It will give you speed and spin while your technique develops. Try a tacky rubber on the forehand later, once your loop (a heavy topspin stroke) is reliable and you play often, ideally with a coach watching. You do not have to use the same type on both sides; a tacky rubber on the forehand, where there is most room for a full stroke, and a tensor on the backhand is one common mix. Whatever you try, change one thing at a time so you can tell what made the difference.
